sessions.title: Structured Pedagogy and Competency-Based Curriculum in Foundational Learning

content.text: By the end of the session, participants should be able to:
Explain what Structured Pedagogy is.
Explain what a Competency-Based Curriculum is.
Describe why both are important for foundational literacy and numeracy.
Explain how Structured Pedagogy and a Competency-Based Curriculum work together to improve learning.
Imagine that a teacher completes every page in the Teacher Guide, but many learners still cannot read simple words or recognise basic quantities.
Has successful learning taken place?
Is completing the lesson the same as learners developing the intended skill?
Take 2–3 responses.
Good teaching requires us to think about both:
how instruction is organised and delivered, and
what learners should know and be able to do as a result.
Structured Pedagogy = How teaching and support are organised
Competency-Based Curriculum = What learners should know, understand and be able to demonstrate
What comes to mind when you hear “Structured Pedagogy”?
Take 2 responses.
Structured Pedagogy is an organised approach to improving classroom teaching by ensuring that the key elements of instruction work together.
It typically includes:
clearly sequenced lessons;
Teacher Guides;
Pupil Books and Teaching and Learning Materials;
explicit instructional routines;
teacher training;
coaching and ongoing support;
classroom assessment; and
use of assessment information to improve teaching.
Structured Pedagogy

Teacher Guide
↓
Pupil Materials/TLMs
↓
Training
↓
Classroom Instruction
↓
Assessment
↓
Coaching & Support
Structured Pedagogy does not simply mean giving teachers a scripted guide.
The strength comes from ensuring that:
curriculum;
materials;
training;
teaching;
assessment; and
ongoing support
are aligned and working together.
Why Is It Important in Foundational Learning?
Foundational literacy and numeracy skills develop progressively.
For example:
Literacy
Letter Sounds → Blending → Word Reading → Sentence Reading → Comprehension
Numeracy
Quantity → Counting → Numeral Recognition → Number Relationships → Operations → Problem Solving
If important steps are skipped, learners may struggle with later skills.
Structured Pedagogy helps teachers:
teach skills in a logical sequence;
use consistent instructional routines;
provide sufficient practice;
use appropriate learning materials;
check learner understanding;
identify learners who need additional support; and
maintain greater consistency across classrooms and schools.
Structured Pedagogy provides teachers with a clear pathway for delivering effective instruction.
What does it mean for a learner to be competent in a skill?
Take 2 responses.
A Competency-Based Curriculum focuses on what learners should be able to demonstrate, rather than only the content a teacher has covered.
A competency brings together:
Knowledge – What does the learner know?
Skills – What can the learner do?
Attitudes/Values – How does the learner apply learning appropriately?
KNOW + DO + DEMONSTRATE = COMPETENCY

content.label: Example
content.text: Literacy
It is not enough for a learner to know the names of letters.
A literacy competency may require the learner to:
recognise letter sounds and use them to blend and read words.

content.label: Example
content.text: Numeracy
It is not enough for a learner to recite:
The learner may need to:
count five objects accurately and match the quantity to numeral 5.
The focus therefore moves from:
“Did I teach it?”
to:
“Can the learner demonstrate it?

blocks.title: Why Is Competency-Based Learning Important for Foundational Learning?

content.text: Foundational learning is about building essential skills that learners need for later learning.
Competency-based teaching helps teachers focus on whether learners can actually:
In Literacy
identify sounds;
blend;
segment;
read words;
read connected text;
understand what they read;
express ideas orally and in writing.
In Numeracy
recognise quantities;
count accurately;
recognise numerals;
compare numbers;
understand number relationships;
add and subtract;
solve simple problems.
If a learner cannot demonstrate an earlier skill, should the teacher simply continue because the lesson schedule says so?
Take responses.
The curriculum provides the intended progression.
Assessment helps teachers know whether learners are developing the competencies.
Learners who are struggling may need additional practice, remediation or differentiated support.
Competency-based teaching focuses on demonstrated learning, not simply content coverage.

blocks.title: How Do Structured Pedagogy and Competency-Based Curriculum Work Together?

rows: Defines what learners should know and do
Organises how teaching supports learners to achieve it
Supports teachers to achieve consistent instruction

content.text: The two approaches complement each other.
Competency-Based Curriculum tells us WHERE learners need to go.
Structured Pedagogy provides a PATHWAY for helping them get there.
COMPETENCY
What should learners know and do?
STRUCTURED INSTRUCTION
How will we teach it?
PRACTICE
How will learners develop the skill?
ASSESSMENT
Can learners demonstrate it?
RESPONSE
Proceed, practise more, differentiate or remediate
What is the difference between Structured Pedagogy and a Competency-Based Curriculum?
Competency-Based Curriculum = the learning learners must demonstrate.
Structured Pedagogy = the organised teaching, materials, assessment and support used to help learners achieve that learning.
In this session, we will discuss why it is important for learners in ECD and Lower Basic to learn to read in a familiar Gambian National Language.
By the end of the session, you will be able to:
Explain why it is important for children to learn to read in Gambian National Languages.

blocks.title: Why Reading in a Familiar Language Matters

content.text: There is strong research evidence from Africa and elsewhere supporting the use of a familiar language when children are beginning to learn to read and write.
Learning to read is a challenging process. It can be easier for learners when they begin in a language they already speak and understand well.
When learners begin reading in a familiar Gambian National Language, they can connect the words and ideas they already know through speaking and listening with the written form of the language.
This can help learners understand what they read, participate more confidently in literacy activities, and develop important foundational reading and writing skills.
Many of these literacy skills can later support learners when they begin learning to read and write in English.
Teaching early literacy in a familiar Gambian National Language therefore provides an important foundation for literacy development in both the National Language and English.
When we say a learner can “read,” what exactly do we mean?
Think about this for a moment.
Ask participants to turn to a partner and discuss:
What does a learner need to be able to do for us to say that they can read?
Give pairs 1 minute.
Take 2–3 quick responses.
Reading involves more than saying the words on a page.
Learners need to be able to read the words and understand what those words mean.
Ask participants to open to the “What is Reading?” section in the resource packet.
Invite one participant to read aloud the first three sentences under “What is Reading?”
Let participants read out the complete equation for reading “Sound + Meaning = Reading”.
When we add these two elements together, we can say we are truly reading!
If someone knows the sounds of the word “cat” and can say it, but doesn’t know what “cat” means, is that reading? No!

For example, if someone can hear the word cat and see a cat in their head or think about a time that they have played with a cat, but they cannot see the word “cat” on a page and say it, is that reading? No!

In the simple view of reading, we know that learners need to know how to read a word using letter sounds and how to think about and understand what they read. The Gambia FL programme materials teach learners how to do this.
We know there are many skills that learners require to be strong readers. We can organize those skills into six categories that we call the Components of Reading.
Ask participants to open Components of Reading under “What is Reading?” in the resource packet.
Ask volunteer participants in each group to read aloud the descriptions of each of the components of reading.

rows:
Separate and tell the difference between sounds they hear and say:
Say:
[Note: Phonological awareness is ONLY about sounds. Nothing is written on the board when practicing phonological awareness. All you need is your ears and mouth – you can practice phonological awareness with your eyes closed.

Connect sounds with letters and blend sounds together to read words.
Say:
[Note: Phonics is about connecting what is heard to what is seen. You need your eyes/skill of braille reading and your ears to practice phonics skills.
Determine the meanings of words and use a variety of words to express ideas.
Read text with appropriate speed, accuracy, intonation, and expression (Prosody).
Understand the events, characters, and messages in a text. Analyze text in different ways.

Explain that there are other skills that support reading that learners need to develop:
Understand how text works (left to right, top to bottom, punctuation).
Speaking and listening skills (expressing ideas clearly, following instructions, etc.)

content.text: Read each short example and ask participants to identify the component.

Example 1:
 “A learner hears the word sun and identifies that it begins with /s/.”
Answer: Phonological awareness

Example 2:
 “A learner sees the letter s, says /s/, and blends sounds to read a word.”
Answer: Phonics

Example 3:
 “A learner explains what the word enormous means.”
Answer: Vocabulary

Example 4:
 “A learner reads a sentence smoothly and with expression.”
Answer: Fluency

Example 5:
 “A learner explains why a character in a story was unhappy.”
Answer: Comprehension
Think about one learner you currently teach. Which component of reading is strongest for that learner, and which component may require more support?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 2 minutes.
Invite 2 participants to share.
Ask each participant to identify both:
the reading component; and
one way they currently support it.
Strong reading develops through several interconnected skills.
Throughout the training, we will look more closely at how to teach and strengthen these skills.

sessions.title: Steps of Word Reading
materials: Letter Cards (two - two letters that can blend)

content.text: In this session we will be talking about:
The skills learners need to read words.
The process of word reading.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Describe the key steps learners use to read words.
Demonstrate strategies for supporting learners to blend sounds into syllables and syllables into words.

blocks.title: Introduction: How Do We Read an Unfamiliar Word?

content.text: Reading a word involves several skills working together.
Before learners can read words independently, they need to recognise the letters or symbols, know the sounds they represent, and combine those sounds to form syllables and words.
Let us experience what this can feel like for a beginning reader.
Ask participants to open to the “Mystery Words” activity in the Resource Packet.
Ask pairs to use the key to work out one mystery word.
Give them 1 minute.
Ask one participant:
What steps did you use to work out the word?
Take 2–3 quick responses.
You first identified what each symbol represented, connected it to a sound, and then combined the sounds to read the word.
Learners go through a similar process when learning to read unfamiliar words.
For beginning readers, we can think about word reading as a progression:
1. Recognise the letter
2. Recall the letter sound
3. Blend sounds to read a syllable
4. Blend syllables to read a word
5. Read the word automatically
If a learner has difficulty at one step, the teacher needs to identify that difficulty and provide support at that level.
For example, asking a learner to blend a word will be difficult if the learner does not yet know the sounds represented by the letters.
If a learner cannot blend /r/ and /i/ to make “ri”, what might the teacher need to check first?
Take 1–2 responses.
Whether the learner recognises the letters.
Whether the learner knows the corresponding sounds
Once learners know the sounds represented by letters, we help them bring those sounds together.
This is called blending.
ri
Cover i and show r.
Ask participants to say the sound: /r/
Cover r and show i.
Ask participants to say: /i/
Point to both sounds from left to right:
Run your finger smoothly underneath the syllable and ask participants to say:
ri
Repeat with one additional example, such as:
la
Notice that we first helped learners identify each sound and then gradually brought the sounds together.
This is scaffolding. As learners become stronger readers, we gradually reduce this support.
Word Reading – Blending Syllables
Once learners can read syllables, they can combine syllables to read longer words.
si | ma
Cover ma and ask participants to read si.
Cover si and ask them to read ma.
Point to both:
si – ma
Run your finger underneath the whole word:
sima
The process is:
Word Reading Strategies

Use a simple example.
Hold up one hand.
Touch one finger for the first sound.
Touch another finger for the second sound.
Say each sound.
Sweep across the fingers while blending the sounds together.
This gives learners a physical way of keeping track of individual sounds before bringing them together.
It can be useful for learners who need additional support with blending.
Now, you will work with a partner to practice these words reading strategies.
Write the following syllables on the board:
ba ta pe ma ne lo do fi bi ku nu

Ask participants to turn to a person next to them and work together to blend the sounds in each syllable. Then, they should build as many words as they can out of the syllables by blending them together. They must create real words in their national languages.
After 3 minutes, ask 2 pairs to share one word they built. Write each word on the board.
Demonstrate blending syllables and sounds of each word:
Cover syllables/letters to demonstrate blending
Use “tapping out”
What do your learners do when they find a word they do not know in a text?
What strategies do they use? What are their challenges?
Ask participants to turn to a partner to discuss how learners struggle with word reading.
After 5 minutes, invite 3-4 participants to share their answers.

In this session, we will look at three important skills that help learners read and write words: sounding, blending and segmenting.
Learners need to recognise letter sounds, blend sounds together to read words, and segment words into individual sounds when spelling and writing.
By the end of the session, you will be able to:
Describe how sounding, blending and segmenting support word reading and writing.
Demonstrate strategies for teaching sounding, blending and segmenting.
Think about how a young child learns to walk. Does the child begin by running immediately?
Learning to read is also gradual. Learners develop foundational skills step by step and need repeated practice and support.

In the same way, learners build reading skills progressively. They first learn sounds, then combine those sounds to read syllables and words.

sessions.title: Differences Between English (L2) and The Gambian National Languages (L1)

content.text: In this session, we will explore:
some important differences between English and Gambian National Languages;
how these differences can affect learners when learning to read in English; and
practical ways teachers can support learners as they develop English language and reading skills.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Describe key differences between English and Gambian National Languages and explain how these may affect learning to read in English.
Identify practical strategies for supporting learners to develop English as a second language.
English and Gambian National Languages differ in several ways, including their sounds, spelling patterns, word structures and sentence structures.
These differences can influence how learners transfer what they already know from their familiar language when learning to read English.
What is one difference you have noticed between English and the Gambian National Language you speak or teach?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 2 minutes.
Take 2–3 responses.
Some English sounds do not occur in some Gambian National Languages, for example “th.”
Letters may represent different sounds across languages.
English has less predictable letter-sound relationships.
Sentence structures may differ.
Some Gambian National Languages do not distinguish masculine and feminine pronouns in the same way as English.
Languages differ in both their spoken and written structures, and these differences can affect how learners learn to read a second language.
There are three important differences we need to consider.
A. Sounds
Languages do not always use the same sounds.
Some English sounds may not exist in a learner's Gambian National Language.
For example, the English “th” sound may be unfamiliar to learners who do not use this sound in their first language.
B. Letter-Sound Relationships
Gambian National Languages generally have more predictable relationships between written letters and their sounds.
English is less predictable.
In English, the same letter can represent different sounds.
For example:
c in cat
c in city
English also has letter combinations whose pronunciation varies.
C. Grammar and Sentence Structure
Languages may organize words and sentences differently.
For example, the position of words such as prepositions may differ between English and some Gambian National Languages.
Pronouns and other grammatical structures may also differ.

These differences mean that learners cannot always apply everything they know about their first language directly to English. Some knowledge transfers, while some English-specific features must be explicitly taught.
Based on these differences, what difficulties might a learner experience when learning to read or speak English?
Allow pairs 2 minutes to identify one challenge.
Take 2–3 responses.
Learners may:
find unfamiliar English sounds difficult to pronounce;
apply the sound of a letter from their Gambian National Language when reading English;
find some English spelling patterns difficult;
transfer sentence structures from L1 into English;
struggle to understand a text because they do not yet know enough English vocabulary.
These are normal challenges when learning another language. Teachers should therefore avoid automatically interpreting difficulties with English as evidence of a reading difficulty.
Because learners are developing both English language proficiency and English literacy, teachers need to provide explicit and gradual support.
Some important strategies include:
1. Develop oral language before and alongside reading
Give learners frequent opportunities to listen to and speak English.
Use songs, rhymes, chants, dialogues and structured conversations.
2. Teach English vocabulary explicitly
Introduce important words before learners encounter them in a text.
Use pictures, objects, actions and familiar examples to explain meaning.
3. Explicitly teach English sounds and spelling patterns
Draw attention to sounds or patterns that are different from the learner's Gambian National Language.
Provide repeated opportunities to hear, say, read and write them.
4. Build on what learners already know
Make connections between Gambian National Languages and English where skills are similar.
Clearly point out differences where the languages do not work in the same way.
5. Provide repeated practice
Give learners many opportunities to practise new English vocabulary, sounds and reading patterns.
Choose one of these strategies. What would it look like in an actual English lesson?
Take 2 responses.
We have seen that learning to read in English can present additional challenges because English and Gambian National Languages differ in their sounds, spelling patterns and grammatical structures.
What is one difference between English and a Gambian National Language that teachers need to pay particular attention to, and what can the teacher do to support learners?
Participants discuss with a partner for 2 minutes.
Take 2–3 responses.

The key message is that learners bring valuable language knowledge from their Gambian National Languages. Our role is to build on what transfers, explicitly teach what is different, and provide sufficient oral-language, vocabulary and reading practice in English.

actions;
enjoyment;
practising it many times;
learning with other children.
These same features make songs, rhymes, chants and dialogues useful for learning a second language.

blocks.title: Why Use Rhymes, Songs, Chants and Dialogues?

content.text: Songs, rhymes, chants and dialogues give learners repeated opportunities to hear and use English. E. g. The National Pledge. The Song “Now the day is over.” The National Anthem, etc.
Their repetition helps learners remember new words, phrases and sentence patterns.
Rhythm, actions, facial expressions and gestures help learners connect language with meaning.
Whole-class and group participation can encourage learners who may be shy or less confident to speak.
These activities can also make language learning enjoyable and increase learners’ willingness to participate.
Dialogues provide practice with short, useful expressions and sentence structures that learners can use in meaningful situations.
“What language skill could a learner practise through a song or dialogue?”
Take 2–3 responses, for example:
vocabulary;
pronunciation;
listening;
speaking;
sentence patterns.
Guidelines for Teaching the Rhymes and Chants
When introducing a song, rhyme, chant or dialogue, follow these four steps:
1. Listen
Teacher models the complete song, rhyme, chant or dialogue.
Learners listen first.
2. Understand
Check understanding.
Explain important words and phrases.
Use the Gambian National Language where necessary to clarify meaning.
3. Practise
Learners repeat gradually.
Use clapping, actions, gestures, facial expressions or role play where appropriate.
Pay attention to pronunciation.
4. Perform and Repeat
Learners practise as a whole class, in groups, pairs and eventually with reduced teacher support.
Repeat the activity during subsequent lessons so that learners become increasingly confident and automatic.
Facilitator to choose a Song or Chant or Rhyme from Lessons 1, 6, 11, 16, 21 in the teacher guide and demonstrate teaching it to participants.
For example:

Step 1 – Listen:
 The facilitator performs it once.

Step 2 – Understand:
 Explain 1–2 key words or phrases.

Step 3 – Practise:
 Participants repeat with actions or appropriate expressions.

Step 4 – Perform:
 The whole group performs with reduced facilitator support.
Notice that we did not begin by asking learners to repeat something they did not understand.
We first modelled the language, checked meaning, provided guided practice and then increased learner participation.
Demonstration
Put participants into pairs or small groups.
Ask them to select one short song, rhyme, chant or dialogue from the Teacher Guide.
Give groups 3 minutes to prepare how they would introduce it using:
Repeat
Invite one group to demonstrate for approximately 2 minutes.
Give one brief piece of facilitator feedback.
Observation prompts
Ask participants watching to consider:
Was meaning established?
Was pronunciation modelled clearly?
Were learners actively involved?
Was there sufficient repetition?
Were actions or expressions meaningful?
What is one thing you will do when using songs, rhymes, chants or dialogues to ensure learners are learning English rather than simply repeating words?
Take 2–3 responses.
establish meaning;
model clearly;
provide repetition;
involve learners actively;
connect words with actions/context;
gradually reduce teacher support.
Songs, rhymes, chants and dialogues are not simply entertainment. When used purposefully, they provide repeated and meaningful opportunities for learners to hear, practise and use English.
In this session, we will explore the different types of texts used in the Gambia Foundational Learning materials and how each supports reading development.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Distinguish between fiction and non-fiction texts.
Explain the purpose of Read Aloud and decodable texts.
Locate Read Aloud and decodable texts in the Teacher Guide and Pupil Book.
Introduction

blocks.title: Why Do Learners Need Different Texts?

content.text: Learners need regular opportunities to interact with different types of texts to develop reading skills.
Different texts serve different purposes.
Some texts allow learners to listen to richer language and develop comprehension and vocabulary, while others allow them to practise reading words independently.
What kinds of texts do learners encounter in your classroom?
There are two broad categories of text that learners will encounter:
Fiction
Stories that are mainly imagined or created by an author.
They may contain characters, settings, events and a plot.
Non-Fiction
Texts that provide factual information about real people, places, objects, events or ideas.

content.label: Do
content.text: Quick Check
Read two examples and ask participants to call out:
Fiction or Non-Fiction?
“A clever rabbit tricked the lion.”
Fiction
“The River Gambia flows through The Gambia.”
Non-Fiction
Both fiction and non-fiction can be used to develop vocabulary and comprehension.
In the Foundational Learning materials, texts may also be used differently depending on who is doing the reading and the instructional purpose.
What is Read Aloud?
A Read Aloud is a text that the teacher reads aloud to learners.
It may be more complex than the text learners can currently read independently.
This allows learners to hear rich language while the teacher models fluent and expressive reading.
Read Aloud texts also introduce vocabulary and provide opportunities to develop comprehension.
The Teacher Guide includes prompts that help teachers engage learners before, during and after reading.
Read Aloud
Who reads?Where is it?Main purpose?
Ask participants to locate one Read Aloud in their Teacher Guide.
Give them 1 minute.
Then demonstrate a very short example:
Before Reading
“Look at the picture. What do you think this story might be about?”
During Reading
“What do you think will happen next?”
After Reading
“Why do you think the character did that?”
Notice that learners are not passive during a Read Aloud.
The teacher reads, but learners are listening, predicting, answering questions, learning vocabulary and thinking about meaning.
A decodable text is designed around letter-sound relationships and word patterns that learners have already been taught.
Unlike a Read Aloud, learners are expected to do the reading themselves.
The purpose is to give learners practice applying their phonics and word-reading skills.
Decodable Text
Who reads?Where is it?Main purpose?
Decodable texts mainly contain:
phonics patterns already taught;
previously taught high-frequency words;
increasingly complex spelling patterns as learners progress.
Ask participants to turn to Lessons 31-35 in the Pupil Book.
Ask them to look for and point to the title of the Decodable
Text.
If a learner struggles with a word in a decodable text, should the teacher immediately read the word for the learner?
No.
The teacher should support the learner to use the sounds and word-reading strategies already taught.
The goal is to develop independent reading.
This comparison should become the key summary of the session.

rows: Can be above learners' independent reading level
Based largely on taught phonics patterns
Model fluent reading and engage learners in meaning

content.text: Ask pairs:
A teacher wants learners to practise a newly taught letter-sound pattern independently. Which text should the teacher use, and why?
Give 1 minute.
Decodable text, because it gives learners an opportunity to apply previously taught phonics skills independently.
If the teacher wants to introduce richer vocabulary and model fluent reading, which text would be more appropriate?
Read Aloud.
Both types of text are important, but they have different instructional purposes.
In a Read Aloud, the teacher reads and models while learners develop language and comprehension.
In a decodable text, learners read and practise applying the phonics and word-reading skills they have already learned.
In this session, we will look at how the Gambia Foundational Learning materials systematically help learners move from recognising letters and sounds to reading syllables and words.
We will use activities from the Teacher Guide and Pupil Book to understand the purpose of these drills.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Explain the purpose of the phonics, syllable and word-reading drills in the Gambia Foundational Learning materials.
Demonstrate how these drills support learners to progress from letter sounds to reading words.

blocks.title: From Letters and Sounds to Words

content.text: To read words, learners need to connect the letters they see with the sounds they hear.
They then combine these sounds to read syllables and combine syllables to read words.
The activities in the Pupil Book provide repeated practice at each of these stages.
Ask participants to open to page 1 of the Pupil Book.
Ask them to quickly identify:
the target letter;
the keyword and illustration;
the syllable-reading activity; and
the word-reading activity.
These activities are deliberately connected. They help learners gradually move from recognising a letter and its sound to using that knowledge to read.
Phonics teaches learners the relationship between written letters and the sounds they represent.
The target letter, keyword and illustration work together to help learners remember the sound.
For example:
Learners should see the letter, hear and say the sound, and connect the sound with a familiar keyword and illustration.
This connection supports both reading and writing.
Ask participants to locate Lesson 31 in the Teacher Guide.
The facilitator briefly models the routine using the Teacher Guide and Pupil Book.
Participants then practise the routine with a partner for 2 minutes.
Invite one participant to demonstrate one part of the routine.
Facilitator Note
ECD 2 and 3 participants should make the connection to the corresponding letter/sound activity in the Community/Welcome Circle rather than completing a separate activity during this short session.
Once learners know the sounds represented by letters, they need practice combining those sounds.
Syllables provide an important bridge between individual sounds and whole words.
Ask participants to locate the “Read Syllables” activity in the Teacher Guide and corresponding Pupil Book page.
Model one example:
Point to the first letter and say its sound.
Point to the next letter and say its sound.
Move your finger underneath the letters from left to right.
Blend the sounds together to read the syllable.
Participants practise one example with a partner.
The purpose of the syllable drill is to give learners repeated practice in blending letter sounds together before they encounter longer words.
When learners can read individual syllables, we help them combine those syllables to read words.
For example:
The word-reading drill gives learners repeated opportunities to apply the same blending process to complete words.
Use one word from the Pupil Book.
Cover all but the first syllable.
Ask participants to read it.
Reveal and read the second syllable.
Clap to each syllable:
ba – ta
Run your finger underneath the whole word and blend:
bata
Pair Practice
Ask participants to use one word from the Pupil Book.
Partner A plays the teacher and models the routine.
Partner B plays the learner.
Switch roles after approximately 1 minute.
The progression therefore becomes:
Reflection
If a learner is struggling to read the words in the Pupil Book, which earlier skill would you check first, and why?
Take 2–3 responses.
Teachers need to identify where the difficulty begins.
If learners do not know the target sound, they will struggle to blend syllables. If they cannot read syllables, they are likely to struggle with words.
This is why each drill should be taught carefully and systematically.
In this session, we will discuss:
how pupils progressively develop writing skills;
practical activities for developing handwriting, spelling and written expression; and
how teachers can assess pupils’ writing to determine what support they need.
By the end of the session, you will be able to:
Describe the key skills involved in writing.
Identify activities that support pupils’ writing development.
Identify appropriate ways to assess pupils’ writing skills.
What is Writing?
Writing is the process of communicating ideas through print.
Writing involves more than handwriting.
Writing = Forming Letters + Writing Words + Expressing Ideas
To become successful writers, pupils progressively learn to:
form letters correctly;
use letter-sound knowledge to spell words;
use spaces, capital letters and punctuation;
write sentences; and
communicate their own ideas in writing.
Reading and writing support each other. Pupils can use the sounds, vocabulary and ideas they learn during reading when they write.
Pupils’ writing also gives teachers useful information about what they have learnt and what requires further support.
Is a pupil who can copy letters neatly necessarily a good writer? Why or why not?
Take 2 responses.
Handwriting is one part of writing, but writing also involves spelling, conventions and expressing meaning.
Stages of Reading and Writing
Pupils’ writing develops progressively.

rows: Uses known letter sounds to attempt words
Writes words and sentences with increasing accuracy and conventions
Communicates ideas more independently and clearly

content.text: Show the participants a selection of 4 pictures showing a pupil’s
writing in their Resource Packet.
Which stage might this pupil be at, and what evidence makes you think so?
Take one response for each sample.
The purpose of recognising these stages is not simply to label pupils.
It helps teachers decide what support the pupil needs next.
Handwriting
Handwriting involves forming letters clearly and correctly.
Pupils gradually develop the fine-motor control needed to hold writing tools and form letters.
When teachers introduce a letter and its sound, they can also teach pupils how to form that letter.

content.label: Do
content.text: Quick Demonstration
Use the letter k, as in the original guide.
Write k clearly on the board.
Demonstrate the starting point and direction of movement.
Ask participants to:
trace the letter in the air with a finger;
trace it on the table; and
write it once on paper.
Linking Spelling with Phonics
Spelling is the ability to use letter-sound relationships to write words.
In most Gambian languages, all letters pronounced are written. In English, this isn’t always the case.
For spelling, it’s important that pupils learn to use their knowledge of letter sounds to write words correctly.
It’s always best to combine phonics instruction with spelling instruction.
For example, when you’re teaching pupils that the letters “n” and “g” make the /ng/ sound together, have them practice writing words with this sound.
You can also show pupils how to use syllable segmentation skills to “hear” each syllable in a word. This will make it easier for them to correctly write longer words.
Modeling Writing
Even before pupils are at the stage where they are writing their own sentences, pupils can write stories together with the teacher.
Modelling writing helps pupils see the steps a writer goes through.
How does a teacher-led writing activity likely to support pupils’ development of writing skills?
Let participants discuss in pairs/groups and come out with some of the activities to support writing in ECD2, ECD 3 and G1.
Responses should include:
1. Copying simple letters.
2. Copying/writing words and sentences.
3. Filling in missing letters in words.
4. Filling in blanks in sentences.
5. Correction of sentences.
6. Completion of sentences.
7. Adding new words.
8. Adding sentences.
9. Writing responses to questions.
10. Writing an essay on simple topics.
11. Developing their ideas about topics and writing about them.
In groups, let participants select 3 of the activities above, discuss and demonstrate how to teach them in their class.
Select 2-3 groups to demonstrate.
Because of the many types of writing skills there are several assessment activities that exist to assess these skills.
Letter dictation can be used to assess if pupils know how to
write their letters.
Word dictation can be used to assess spelling (words).
Syllable or word dictation can be used to assess pupils’
phonics and phonological awareness skills.
Sentence dictation can assess pupils’ spelling and text conventions.

A free writing activity is one of the best ways to assess if pupils are applying all of their writing skills. There are many writing prompts to choose from for a free writing activity. For example, a teacher could give pupils the following prompts:
Write a few sentences on the following:
On your way to school ---
My pet ---
What I like about the story is ---
If I were a cat ---
Think about pupils in your class. Which writing area requires the most support: handwriting, encoding/spelling, or expressing ideas? What is one activity you could use to strengthen it?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 1 minute.
Take 2 responses.
Effective writing instruction develops progressively from forming letters, to encoding words, to communicating ideas.
Assessment helps us identify where pupils are and decide what we need to teach next
In this session, we will look at practical strategies for developing learners’ vocabulary and comprehension when using Read Aloud and Learner/Decodable Texts.
We will focus on what teachers do before, during and after reading.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Identify key strategies for developing vocabulary and comprehension before, during and after reading.
Demonstrate a short vocabulary and comprehension activity using a text from the Teacher Guide or Pupil Book.
Reading is not only about recognising words. Learners also need to understand the words and ideas in a text.
Vocabulary and comprehension are therefore developed across reading activities.
In the Gambia Foundational Learning materials, teachers support comprehension before, during and after reading.
What might happen if a learner can read the words in a story but does not understand the vocabulary?
Take 2 quick responses.
This is why vocabulary support is closely connected to comprehension.
Before reading, teachers prepare learners to understand the text.
Two important strategies are:
1. Teach Key Vocabulary
Identify important unfamiliar words.
Explain meaning using:
gestures;
pictures;
objects;
simple explanations;
examples in context.
2. Make Predictions
Use the title, illustrations or key words to help learners think about what the text may be about.

content.label: Do
content.text: Quick Practice
Give participants a title or phrase, for example:
“On My First Day at School”
What might this text be about?
What two words might learners need to understand before reading?
Take 2–3 responses.
The purpose of before-reading activities is to activate what learners already know and prepare them for the language and ideas they will meet in the text.
During reading, the teacher helps learners stay actively engaged with meaning.
Important strategies include:
Think aloud: model what a reader is thinking.
Visualise: encourage learners to imagine what they can see, hear or feel from the story.
Check understanding: ask short questions during reading.
Read with expression: use appropriate tone, pacing and expression to support meaning.
Read or display a very short sentence from a familiar text.
For example:
“Fatou looked at the dark clouds and began to run home.”
What might Fatou be thinking?
What do you think might happen next?
These questions help learners stay mentally involved in the text rather than simply listening passively.
After reading, learners need opportunities to show and deepen their understanding.
Useful strategies include:
retelling or summarising;
drawing;
discussing new vocabulary;
role play;
connecting the story to their own lives;
answering questions.
What is one activity you could use after reading to check whether learners understood the text?
Take 2–3 quick responses.
The activity selected should give the teacher evidence of what learners understood.
Teachers can ask different types of questions after or during reading:

rows: What it asks learners to do
Find information directly stated in the text
Use information in the text and what they already know to work out an answer
Use the text, reasoning and personal experience to form an answer

content.text: Example
For a story where a child carries an umbrella:
Literal:
What was the child carrying?
Inferential:
Why do you think the child carried an umbrella?
Critical Thinking:
What would you have done if you were the child?
Using different types of questions encourages learners to move from recalling information to thinking more deeply about the text.
Which of the three stages, before, during or after reading, do you think teachers most often overlook, and what is one strategy you can use to strengthen it?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 1 minute.
Take 2 responses.
Strong vocabulary and comprehension instruction happens throughout reading:

Before Reading: Prepare
During Reading: Engage and Monitor
After Reading: Check and Extend Understanding
Learning to read in English can be challenging for learners who are still developing their oral English.
Teachers can make English lessons easier to understand by adjusting how they speak, explain, model and provide opportunities for learners to practise.
In this session, we will focus on practical strategies that can be used during daily English lessons.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Identify practical strategies for supporting learners to understand and participate in English lessons.
Demonstrate how to apply selected strategies during an English reading lesson.

blocks.title: Strategy 1: Make Teacher Language Easy to Process

content.text: When teaching learners who are developing English proficiency:
Speak slowly and clearly
Pronounce words clearly.
Use a natural but manageable pace.
Give learners time to process what they hear.
Use short and clear instructions
Instead of long explanations, break information into short chunks.
For example:
Instead of:
“I would like everybody to take out their books and turn to the page we were working on yesterday so that we can continue.”
“Take out your book. Open to page 10.”
Allow wait time
Ask the question.
Pause.
Allow learners time to think and prepare a response.
Then invite a learner to answer.
The original guide emphasises that learners need additional processing time both to understand spoken English and formulate responses.
Give participants one long classroom instruction.
How could you make this instruction shorter and clearer for an English learner?
Take one response.
This combines:
Teach vocabulary.
Use colourful images.
Use many visuals.
Use real objects.
Use gestures and actions.
Learners understand English more easily when teachers connect spoken words with something they can see, touch or experience.
Important vocabulary should be introduced before learners encounter it in a text.
Teachers can use:
pictures;
illustrations;
real objects;
gestures;
facial expressions;
actions;
simple drawings;
familiar examples.

The original session recommends explicit vocabulary teaching and linking words to pictures, definitions and contextual examples. It also recommends visual aids and real objects to make concepts more meaningful.

content.label: Do
content.text: Quick Demonstration
Use the word:
inflate
How could you teach the meaning of “inflate” without giving a long verbal definition?
show a balloon;
blow up the balloon;
use a picture;
demonstrate the action.
The goal is to connect the English word with meaning, not simply ask learners to repeat the word.

blocks.title: Build on What Learners Already Know

content.text: New learning becomes easier when it is connected to something learners already understand.
Before reading, teachers should activate relevant background knowledge.
Where appropriate, familiar Gambian National Languages can help clarify difficult concepts.
Give an example:
The class is going to read a text about a market.
What could the teacher ask before reading to connect the text with learners’ experiences?
Have you been to a market?
What do people sell there?
Who do you go to the market with?
What do you see at the market?
These questions prepare learners to connect familiar experiences with the new English vocabulary and ideas in the text.

blocks.title: Strategy 4: Model Before Asking Learners to Work Independently

content.text: English learners benefit when teachers show them what to do, rather than only explain it verbally.
Use:
I Do: Teacher demonstrates.
We Do: Teacher and learners practise together.
You Do: Learners try independently.
Use a simple vocabulary or reading activity.
For example:
I Do: Teacher demonstrates how to use a new word in a sentence.
We Do: Teacher and learners create another sentence together.
You Do: Learners create their own sentence.
Teachers can also use gestures, actions and examples while modelling.
Support should gradually reduce as learners become more confident.

blocks.title: Strategy 5: Give Learners Opportunities to Use English

content.text: Learners develop English by using English, not only listening to the teacher.
Pair and small-group activities provide learners with more opportunities to practise speaking.
Learners who are reluctant to speak in front of the whole class may feel more comfortable practising with a partner.
The original guide identifies pair and small-group learning as particularly useful for increasing participation and English practice.
Give one example of an English activity learners could practise in pairs.
asking and answering questions;
practising vocabulary;
retelling part of a story;
reading to a partner;
practising dialogue.
Take two responses.
Ask participants to work in pairs.
Give them the following scenario:
You are introducing the word “market” before reading a short English text to Grade 1 learners.
Ask each pair to choose three strategies from the session and demonstrate how they would teach the word.
They might:
speak slowly and clearly;
show a picture;
connect to learners’ experience;
model a sentence;
give learners wait time;
let learners practise with a partner.
Invite one pair to demonstrate briefly.
Which one strategy will you deliberately use more often in your English lessons, and why?
Take 1–2 responses.
Supporting English learners does not mean making learning easier or reducing expectations.
It means making language clear, meaningful and accessible, and giving learners enough support and practice to participate successfully.
Weekly assessment helps teachers understand what pupils can already do and where they need additional support.
In the Gambia Foundational Learning programme, the Assess & Review lesson takes place every fifth day.
Teachers assess selected pupils individually and use the results to guide reinforcement and remediation.
By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Describe the key steps in the weekly Assess & Review process.
Conduct and record a short individual reading assessment using the Teacher Guide.
Use assessment results to identify appropriate follow-up support for pupils.
Teachers cannot provide the right support unless they know what pupils can currently do.
Assessment helps us answer two questions:
1. What can the pupil do now?
2. What does the pupil need help with next?
Assessment is therefore not simply about giving a score. It should inform teaching.
What might happen if a teacher continues teaching without checking what pupils have understood or can do?
Take 2 responses.
Some pupils may need more support.
Others may be ready to progress.
Assessment helps the teacher make those decisions.
Each week, the teacher assesses five pupils individually.
Start from the top of the class list and assess the next five pupils each week.
When the end of the list is reached, begin again from the top.
While the teacher assesses one pupil, the rest of the class rereads the week’s pupil text with a partner.
Weekly Assessment Routine
Whole class:Teacher:Pupil:Teacher:Teacher:Teacher: Decides follow-up support
Ask participants to turn to Lesson 5 in the G1 Teacher Guide.
Point out:
the assessment instructions;
the Assessment Text Annex; and
the scoring information.
Do not ask participants to spend several minutes silently reading all the instructions. The facilitator should direct them to the essential parts.
Teachers need a simple way to record results so they can monitor pupils over time.
At the start of the term, prepare an assessment recording page with pupils’ names.
The same page can be used throughout the term.
Draw a simple example on the board:
The exact percentage should be determined using the table provided under the assessment text in the Teacher Guide.
The important point is that the result is recorded and then used, rather than assessment ending with a number.
Select one participant to act as the pupil.
Use the Week 1 assessment text.
Show the pupil only the assessment text.
Ask the pupil to read aloud.
Listen carefully.
Record words that are:
skipped; or
read incorrectly and not self-corrected.
Do not interrupt to correct the pupil.
Remain encouraging and neutral.
NB: A self-corrected word should not be counted as an error.
During an assessment, the goal is to find out what the pupil can do independently.
If we immediately correct every mistake, we no longer get an accurate picture of the pupil’s current reading ability.
How many errors did you hear?
Take 1–2 responses.
Record the result on the sample recording sheet.
Now you will practise the same routine.
Put participants in pairs.

Partner A: Teacher
 Partner B: Pupil
The “pupil” deliberately makes 2–3 mistakes.
The “teacher”:
listens;
records errors;
checks whether any errors were self-corrected;
records the result.
After approximately 2 minutes, switch roles.
Observation Check
Participants should check:
Did the teacher allow the pupil to read independently?
Did the teacher avoid correcting during the assessment?
Were skipped and incorrectly read words recorded?
Were self-corrections treated as correct?
Assessment becomes useful when teachers act on the results.
The table beneath the assessment text provides suggested interventions according to pupils’ reading accuracy.
Pupils with similar needs can sometimes be grouped together for reinforcement activities.
If several pupils are struggling with the same reading skill, what could the teacher do?
group them for focused practice;
reteach the skill;
provide additional blending or word-reading practice;
monitor them again during future assessments.
Important Facilitator Note

Keep the specific remediation activities from the Teacher Guide/Resource Packet available for participants to consult. The 30-minute session should teach teachers how to use the result to select support, rather than attempting to demonstrate every remediation activity.
The Assess & Review lesson also includes short whole-class checks of spelling and vocabulary after the individual reading assessment.
These should be administered and scored according to the Teacher Guide.
We will not demonstrate both in full during this session because the priority is to understand and practise the overall assessment process.
After assessing a pupil, what is the most important thing the teacher should do with the result?
Take 1–2 responses.
Record it.
Identify the pupil’s needs.
Provide appropriate support.
Monitor progress.
Assessment is useful only when it informs what we teach next.

sessions.title: The “I Do, We Do, You Do” Teaching Strategy for Literacy

content.text: By the end of the session, participants will be able to:
Explain the purpose of the “I Do, We Do, You Do” strategy in literacy instruction.
Describe the teacher and learner roles at each stage.
Demonstrate how the strategy can be used to teach a foundational literacy skill.

blocks.title: Introduction: How Do Learners Develop a New Literacy Skill?

content.text: Think about a learner who is learning to read a word for the first time.
Would we simply show the learner the word and immediately expect them to read it independently?
What support might the learner need first?
Ask participants to discuss with a partner for 1 minute.
Take 2 responses.
When learners are developing a new literacy skill, they often need to:
see and hear the skill modelled;
practise it with support;
practise it independently.
This is the basis of the “I Do, We Do, You Do” teaching strategy.

blocks.title: What Does “I Do, We Do, You Do” Mean?

rows: Models and explains the literacy skill

content.text: The strategy gradually transfers responsibility from the teacher to the learner.
At the beginning, the teacher provides strong support.
As learners demonstrate understanding, the teacher gradually reduces the support.
More Teacher Support
I DO → WE DO → YOU DO
More Learner Independence
Do not move learners to independent practice before they are ready.

blocks.title: Facilitator Demonstration: Blending Sounds to Read Words

content.text: Use one literacy skill throughout the demonstration.

content.label: Skill
content.text: Blending Sounds to Read a Word
Use examples appropriate to the language and previously taught letter sounds in the Teacher Guide.
I Do: Teacher Models
Display the word:
mat
Point to each letter as you model.
“Watch and listen as I read this word.”
Point to m:
Point to a:
Point to t:
Then sweep your finger from left to right underneath the word.
I identified the sound represented by each letter.
Then I blended the sounds together to read the whole word.
During I Do, learners watch and listen while the teacher clearly models the skill.
We Do: Guided Practice
Display another decodable word using previously taught sounds, for example:
sat
“Now let us read this word together.”
Point to s.
“What sound?”
Point to a.
Point to t.
“Now let us blend the sounds together.”
During We Do, learners are doing more of the work, but I am still guiding and supporting them.
I listen carefully so that I can identify and correct errors before learners practise independently.
You Do: Independent Practice
Display a new decodable word containing previously taught sounds, for example:
tap
“Now read this word by yourself.”
Allow learners time to:
identify the sounds;
blend them together; and
read the word.
During You Do, the learner demonstrates whether they can use the skill independently.
The teacher observes and decides whether the learner is ready to continue or needs additional support.

blocks.title: When Should the Teacher Move to the Next Stage?

content.text: The purpose of this session is to ensure that teachers and headteachers have a clear understanding of the programme’s MEL framework, particularly Fidelity of Implementation.
This should help participants:

Why is monitoring important in a programme like RISE Foundational Learning?
Take 2–3 quick responses.
Monitoring helps determine whether the programme is being implemented as intended and where additional support may be required.
In your own words, what is Fidelity of Implementation? What components do you think make up FOI?
Take a few responses before introducing the core MEL concepts. The presentation uses this question to transition into Monitoring, Evaluation, Learning and Theory of Change.
Monitoring
Monitoring is the continuous operational process of tracking performance against programme objectives using specific indicators.
For the RISE Foundational Learning programme, this includes high-frequency data collection such as:
termly School Surveys;
Classroom Observations; and
other implementation monitoring information.
The purpose is to measure progress while implementation is happening.
Evaluation
Evaluation is the systematic assessment of:
programme design;
implementation; and
results.
It takes place at specific intervals, including:
Baseline → Midline → Endline
Evaluation helps determine whether the programme’s Theory of Change is valid, identify external factors affecting results, and generate evidence for policy reform and programme scaling.
Learning
Learning means taking monitoring and evaluation findings and turning them into actionable knowledge.
The programme uses a Learning Agenda and Data Utilization Meetings (DUMs) to support adaptive management.
Adaptive management means:
Using evidence to make necessary programme changes quickly.
Theory of Change
The Theory of Change describes how and why programme activities are expected to lead to the long-term goal of improving foundational learning outcomes for early-grade learners in The Gambia.
The Theory of Change is the programme’s cause-and-effect roadmap.
FOI functions as an early warning system.
Its purpose is to identify whether implementation is following the intended pathway before implementation problems become larger.
Definition
Fidelity of Implementation measures the quality of delivery and adherence to the structured pedagogy model.
For teachers, this includes whether they are:
following scripted lessons;
using the provided Teaching and Learning Materials;
conducting learner assessments as designed.
Four Components of FOI

rows: Following the lesson plan and including the active ingredients of the lesson as designed.
Actively involving learners rather than allowing them to remain passive recipients.
Using learner-centred and inclusive practices, involving learners from different parts of the class, balancing participation of lower- and higher-performing learners, and praising effort.
Delivering lessons with the intended frequency, dosage and duration, including following the time indicated in scripted lesson plans.

sessions.title: Understanding Special Educational Needs and Identifying Learners Who Require Support

content.text: By the end of the session, you will be able to:
Explain the concept of Special Educational Needs (SEN).
Recognize common signs that a learner may be experiencing difficulty with learning, vision, or hearing.
Use observation, questioning, and simple classroom assessment strategies to identify learners who may need additional support.
Describe appropriate first steps for supporting and referring learners.

“Every classroom includes learners with different strengths, experiences, abilities, and ways of understanding the world. Some learners may need additional support to participate fully and make progress.
As teachers, our role is not simply to deliver content. We also create an environment where every learner has the opportunity to learn, participate, and succeed.
Today we will explore what we mean by Special Educational Needs, how we can identify learners who may be struggling, and how we can respond in supportive and respectful ways.
The purpose is not to label learners. It is to help us understand their needs and adapt our teaching so that they can participate and progress.”
Briefly introduce the objectives
“By the end of this session, you should be able to explain SEN, identify possible signs of difficulty, and describe strategies for providing appropriate support.”
“Think of a time when you found learning something difficult. It might have been reading in a new language, solving a mathematics problem, using a new tool, or learning a new skill.”
Give participants one minute to reflect silently.
Ask participants to discuss the following questions with a partner:
1. What made the learning difficult?
2. How did you feel?
3. What helped you?
After the pair discussion, divide participants into four groups. Ask each group to record responses under three headings:
Challenges
Feelings
What helped
Invite each group to share one or two responses.

“Common responses may include feeling confused, frustrated, embarrassed, slow, or left behind. Participants may also mention that demonstrations, visual support, repetition, extra time, encouragement, or a different explanation were helpful.”
Link to the topic

“Learners do not all experience difficulty for the same reason. Some learners experience significant and ongoing barriers that affect how they communicate, learn, move, see, hear, or participate. These learners may have Special Educational Needs.”
“Special Educational Needs refers to learning or participation needs that require additional support, resources, adaptations, or teaching approaches beyond what is normally provided in the classroom.
A learner may need support because of difficulties with:
Reading, writing, or mathematics
Attention, memory, or processing information
Communication or language
Vision or hearing
Physical movement or coordination
Social interaction, emotions, or behaviour
A medical or developmental condition
Having a difficulty does not mean that a learner cannot learn. It means that the learner may need a different approach, additional time, suitable materials, or targeted support.”
“We should not assume that poor performance is caused by laziness or lack of ability. We should observe carefully, identify barriers, try appropriate classroom strategies, and monitor progress.”
Important clarification

“Teachers should not diagnose disabilities. Their role is to notice possible signs, document concerns, provide appropriate classroom support, communicate with families and colleagues, and follow the school’s referral procedures where necessary.”
Give each group one case study, or read the examples aloud.
Case study A: Reading difficulty
“Samuel avoids reading aloud. He reads slowly, loses his place, and often confuses similar letters. He becomes frustrated when asked to complete reading tasks.”
Case study B: Possible vision difficulty
“Amara regularly moves to the front of the classroom, squints at the board, and complains of headaches after copying notes.”
Case study C: Possible hearing difficulty
“David often does not begin tasks after verbal instructions. He watches other learners before starting and sometimes turns one ear toward the teacher.”
Group questions
Ask groups to discuss:
1. What have you observed?
2. What additional information would you need?
3. What could the teacher try immediately?
4. What should the teacher record or communicate?
Allow three minutes for discussion and three minutes for feedback.
Expected responses
Participants may suggest:
Observing the learner in different activities and settings
Speaking privately with the learner
Checking whether instructions were understood
Asking the learner to explain or demonstrate the task
Reviewing the learner’s work over time
Checking seating, lighting, noise, and classroom distractions
Providing visual instructions, demonstrations, repetition, or additional time
Consulting another teacher, the school support team, or the learner’s family
Following the school’s referral process if concerns continue

“Early identification is important because difficulties can become more serious when they are not recognized or addressed. However, identifying a concern does not mean immediately labelling a learner or assuming a diagnosis.”
Practical classroom strategies
Teachers can:
Give short, clear instructions
Present information in different ways
Use pictures, demonstrations, objects, and written instructions
Check understanding by asking learners to explain the task
Provide extra time where appropriate
Seat learners where they can see and hear clearly
Reduce unnecessary background noise
Break large tasks into smaller steps
Provide repetition and guided practice
Pair learners appropriately for peer support
Praise effort, participation, and progress
Keep brief records of observations and strategies used
Referral message
“Specialist services may be needed when a learner’s needs cannot be met through reasonable classroom adaptations or when concerns continue despite support.
Before referring a learner, teachers should:
1. Observe the learner carefully.
2. Record specific examples and patterns.
3. Try appropriate classroom strategies.
4. Monitor the learner’s response.
5. Consult colleagues and communicate respectfully with the family.
6. Follow the school’s established referral procedures.
Other teachers and school staff may also have useful information and strategies. Collaboration is an important part of supporting learners.”
Ask participants to complete an exit ticket by writing:
1. One thing I now understand about SEN is…
2. One sign I will look out for is…
3. One strategy I can use in my classroom is…
Invite two or three participants to share their responses.
“Today we learned that Special Educational Needs relate to barriers that may affect a learner’s ability to access, participate in, or benefit from education.

We also discussed possible signs of learning, vision, and hearing difficulties. A single sign does not confirm a disability. Teachers should observe carefully, avoid assumptions, provide appropriate support, document concerns, and seek further guidance when needed.
The goal is not to label or ‘fix’ learners. The goal is to understand their needs, remove barriers, and create opportunities for every learner to participate and succeed.”
Key takeaway
Observe carefully. Support appropriately. Record accurately. Refer responsibly.
